entries.lesson_core_move: Recognize time invariance by interpreting whether delaying or advancing any continuous-time input causes the system output to undergo the identical delay or advance without changing shape or rule.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Matching Output Delay

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=2x(t-1)$ and delay $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$, which pair is the correct time-shift-then-system and system-then-shift comparison?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For TTS, replace $x(t)$ with $x(t-T)$ inside $y(t)=2x(t-1)$ to get $2x((t)-1-T)$. For STS, form $y_{sts}(t)=y(t-T)=2x((t-T)-1)$. These are identical, so the delayed output matches exactly.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=5x(t+1)$ with input shift $x_1(t)=x(t-2)$, which option correctly shows the two paths and the match status?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{tts}(t)=5x((t)+1-2)=5x(t-1)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=5x((t-2)+1)=5x(t-1)$. The paths match.
$y_{tts}(t)=5x((t+2)-1)=5x(t+1)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=5x((t)-2+1)=5x(t-1)$, so they do not match.
$y_{tts}(t)=5x(t+1-2)=5x(t-1)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=5x((t)-1)=5x(t-1)$. These differ only by the symbol used for the input shift.
$y_{tts}(t)=5x(t+1)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=5x(t-1)$, so the system does not preserve the delayed input.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same compare workflow with fixed gain $5$: $y_{tts}(t)=5x(t+1-2)=5x(t-1)$ from substitution into $x(t-2)$, and $y_{sts}(t)=y(t-2)=5x((t-2)+1)=5x(t-1)$. Both paths are identical, so this is still a matching-output-delay case.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Matching Output Advance

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=3x(t)$ and advanced input $x_1(t)=x(t+T)$, which pair of path outputs is correct?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{tts}(t)=3x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=3x(t+T)$, so the two paths match exactly.
$y_{tts}(t)=3x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=3x(t-T)$, which swaps the shift sign in the second path.
$y_{tts}(t)=3x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=3x(t+T)$, which flips the sign in the first path only.
$y_{tts}(t)=3x((t+T)-1)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=3x(t+T)$, which is applying the system delay in the wrong place.
$y_{tts}(t)=3x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=3x(t+T)+1$, which adds a constant not present in the system rule.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For TTS, substitute the shifted input into the rule: $y_{tts}(t)=3x_1(t)=3x(t+T)$. For STS, shift the unshifted output by $T$: $y(t)=3x(t) \implies y_{sts}(t)=y(t+T)=3x(t+T)$. They match term by term.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$ and $x_1(t)=x(t+2T)$, which pair best shows the matched output advance?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{tts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$, so the outputs are identical.
$y_{tts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t-2T)$, which uses the wrong direction in STS.
$y_{tts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t-2T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$, which flips the sign in the TTS path.
$y_{tts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x((t+2)T)$, which treats $2T$ as a product inside the argument.
$y_{tts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)+3$, which applies extra arithmetic to the output.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The system is $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$. Thus $y_{tts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x_1(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$. The system-then-shift path is $y(t+2T)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+2T)$, so both are identical.

sections.section_title: Recognizing When a Shift Changes the Output Pattern

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=t x(t)$ and delayed input $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$, which pair of expressions is the correct two-path result in the time-variance test?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{tts}(t)=x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=x(t-T)$.
$y_{tts}(t)=t x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=(t-T)x(t-T)$.
$y_{tts}(t)=t x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=t x(t-T)$ after canceling the time shift factors.
$y_{tts}(t)=t x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=(t-T)x(t-T)$, so only the direction of the shift changes.
$y_{tts}(t)=t x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=(t-T)x(t)$, because only the coefficient must shift.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shifted input goes into the same rule, so the first path is $y_{tts}(t)=t x(t-T)$. Shifting the original output gives $y_{sts}(t)=(t-T)x(t-T)$, so the two paths differ. The multiplier becomes $t-T$, so this is not time invariant.

prompt_blocks.text: Now use $x_1(t)=x(t+T)$. Which option correctly states the two-path comparison for $y(t)=t x(t)$ and the resulting classification?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{tts}(t)=t x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=(t+T)x(t+T)$, so the paths do not match and the system is not time invariant.
$y_{tts}(t)=t x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=t x(t+T)$, so the system is time invariant because the output is only shifted.
$y_{tts}(t)=t x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=(t+T)x(t+T)$, because the sign of $T$ cancels in the STS path.
$y_{tts}(t)=x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=x(t+T)$, because $t$ is fixed for this system.
$y_{tts}(t)=t x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=(t+T)x(t-T)$, which matches after replacing $t\to t+T$ in every term.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For advance, $x_1(t)=x(t+T)$ gives $y_{tts}(t)=t x(t+T)$. The shifted original output is $y_{sts}(t)=y(t+T)=(t+T)x(t+T)$. Again the extra $+T$ in the multiplicative time factor changes the rule, so the paths are not identical.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the output produced by first shifting a continuous-time input signal and then applying the system rule, so it can be compared against the system-then-shift path in a time-invariance test.

sections.section_title: Writing the Shifted Input as the System Input

prompt_blocks.text: For the system $y(t)=3x(t)$, the input is first shifted by $x(t-T)$. What is $y_{STS}(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{STS}(t)=3x(t-T)$
$y_{STS}(t)=3x(t+T)$
$y_{STS}(t)=3x(t-T)-T$
$y_{STS}(t)=3x(t)+T$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Define the shifted input as $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ and substitute it directly into the rule: $y(t)=3x(t)$ gives $y_{STS}(t)=3x_1(t)=3x(t-T)$.

prompt_blocks.text: For the system $y(t)=-4x(t)$, if the input is first shifted as $x(t-u)$, what is $y_{STS}(t)$ for the shifted-input step?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: After shift, $x_1(t)=x(t-u)$. The system is still $y(t)=-4x(t)$, so the shifted-input output is $y_{STS}(t)=-4x_1(t)=-4x(t-u)$.

sections.section_title: Applying a Memoryless System Rule After the Input Shift

prompt_blocks.text: For the shifted input $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ and system rule $y(t)=x(t-4)$, what is the shift-then-system output $y_{STS}(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write the shifted input as $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$, then replace every $x(t)$ in the rule with $x(t-T)$: $y_{STS}(t)=x_1(t-4)=x((t-T)-4)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ and the memoryless rule $y(t)=x(t+2)$, find $y_{STS}(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same substitution pattern: $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$, then apply the system rule $y(t)=x(t+2)$ to the shifted input. This gives $y_{STS}(t)=x_1(t+2)=x((t-T)+2)$.

sections.section_title: Applying a System Rule with Internal Input Shifts After the Input Shift

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=x(t-2)-x(t+1)$, find the shift-then-system output when $x(t)$ is first shifted by $T$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$, then substitute in both system arguments: $y_{STS}(t)=x_1(t-2)-x_1(t+1)=x((t-T)-2)-x((t-T)+1)$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=2x(t+4)-x(t-6)$, compute $y_{STS}(t)$ after replacing $x(t)$ with $x(t-T)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ and apply the same rule to each shifted argument: $y_{STS}(t)=2x_1(t+4)-x_1(t-6)=2x((t-T)+4)-x((t-T)-6)$. Only the input arguments shift; the coefficient remains unchanged.

sections.section_title: Applying a Multi-Term System Rule After the Input Shift

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=3x(t-1)+2x(t+1)-5x(t)$, if $x(t)$ is first shifted to $x(t-T)$, what is $y_{STS}(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Start with $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$. The multi-term rule keeps each coefficient fixed and shifts each $x(\cdot)$ argument by replacing $t$ with $t-T$. So $y_{STS}(t)=3x_1(t-1)+2x_1(t+1)-5x_1(t)=3x((t-T)-1)+2x((t-T)+1)-5x(t-T)$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=4x(t-2)-x(t+3)+2x(t)$, when $x(t)$ is first shifted by $T$, what is the shift-then-system output?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$. Substitute $x_1$ into each term and keep constants unchanged: $4x(t-2)-x(t+3)+2x(t)$ becomes $4x_1(t-2)-x_1(t+3)+2x_1(t)$. Replacing $x_1$ gives $4x((t-T)-2)-x((t-T)+3)+2x(t-T)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the system-then-shift path by applying the continuous-time system rule to x(t) to get y(t), then replacing t with t - T to form y(t - T) for comparison in a time-invariance test.

sections.section_title: Applying the System Rule Before Any Input Shift

prompt_blocks.text: For the system $y(t)=3x(t)+x(t-1)$ and input $x(t)=t^2$, first compute $y(t)$ and then find the full shifted-output result $y(t-T)$. Give the fully expanded expression for $y(t-T)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: First, $y(t)=3t^2+(t-1)^2=4t^2-2t+1$. Then replace $t$ with $t-T$ to apply the system-then-shift path, so $y(t-T)=4(t-T)^2-2(t-T)+1=4t^2-8tT+4T^2-2t+2T+1$.

prompt_blocks.text: For the system $y(t)=5x(t)-2x(t-2)$ and input $x(t)=t^2$, first compute $y(t)$ and then form the shifted output $y(t-T)$. Give the fully expanded expression for $y(t-T)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $y(t)=5t^2-2(t-2)^2=3t^2+8t-8$. Shift that final expression by replacing every $t$ with $t-T$: $y(t-T)=3(t-T)^2+8(t-T)-8=3t^2-6tT+3T^2+8t-8T-8$.

sections.section_title: Forming y(t - T) from a Direct Output Expression

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=4t-7$, what is $y(t-T)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For the system-then-shift path, replace every occurrence of $t$ in $y(t)$ with $t-T$ and keep the constant $-7$ unchanged.

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=3t^2-5t+2$, what is $y(t-T)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the same replacement rule: every explicit $t$ in $y(t)$ becomes $t-T$, including each occurrence in the quadratic and linear terms.

sections.section_title: Forming y(t - T) When y(t) Contains x(t - a)

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=x(t-2)+2x(t-4)$, what is $y(t-T)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Shift the finished output by replacing every $t$ with $t-T$, so both arguments become $(t-T)-2$ and $(t-T)-4$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=3x(t-3)-x(t-5)$, what is $y(t-T)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply $t\to t-T$ inside every delayed argument, so $(t-3)$ becomes $t-T-3$ and $(t-5)$ becomes $t-T-5$.

sections.section_title: Forming y(t - T) When y(t) Combines Multiple Terms

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=3x(t-2)-x(t)+2t-5$, what is $y(t-T)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Replace every occurrence of $t$ with $t-T$. The delayed term becomes $x(t-T-2)$, the undelayed term becomes $x(t-T)$, the explicit time term becomes $2(t-T)$, and the constant stays $-5$.
Replace each $t$ in $y(t)$ with $t-T$. Both $x$ arguments shift, and only the free term $-3t$ changes to $-3(t-T)$ while constant $+7$ is unchanged.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compare the shift-then-system and system-then-shift expressions for an arbitrary input shift to classify a continuous-time input-output system as time invariant or time varying.

sections.section_title: Matching Shift-Then-System and System-Then-Shift Expressions

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=3x(t)$ with input shift $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$, which comparison correctly classifies the system?

choice_blocks.text: $y_1(t)=3x(t-T)$, $y_2(t)=3x(t-T)$, and therefore $y_1(t)=y_2(t)$; the system is time invariant.
$y_1(t)=3x(t+T)$, $y_2(t)=3x(t-T)$; this mismatch in shift direction means the paths do not match.
$y_1(t)=3x(t)$ and $y_2(t)=3x(t-T)$; the unshifted path would be skipped in this test.
$y_1(t)=3x(t-T)$, $y_2(t)=3x(t-T+1)$; these expressions are not equal.
$y_2(t)=3x(t-T)$ and no $y_1(t)$ is needed because this is a gain-only system.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Shift first gives $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ and then applying $3\cdot$ gives $y_1(t)=3x(t-T)$. Shifting the original output $y(t)=3x(t)$ by $T$ gives $y_2(t)=3x(t-T)$. Both sides match for arbitrary $T$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=5x(t-1)$ and $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$, identify the correct path comparison and conclusion.

choice_blocks.text: $y_1(t)=5x((t-T)-1)=5x(t-T-1)$ and $y_2(t)=5x((t-T)-1)=5x(t-T-1)$, so they are equal and the system is time invariant.
$y_1(t)=5x((t+T)-1)=5x(t+T-1)$, $y_2(t)=5x((t-T)-1)$, so the advance/de-delay mix causes a mismatch.
$y_1(t)=5x((t-T)-1)$ and only this path is required for the time-invariance test.
$y_1(t)=5x(t-1-T)$, $y_2(t)=5x(t-1-T)-T$; therefore the system is not time invariant.
$y_1(t)=5x(t-1)$, $y_2(t)=5x((t-T)-1)$; because only $y_2$ contains $T$, the system is time varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Start from $y(t)=5x(t-1)$. Shift first gives $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ and $y_1(t)=5x_1(t-1)=5x((t-T)-1)=5x(t-T-1)$. Shift second gives $y_2(t)=y(t-T)=5x((t-T)-1)=5x(t-T-1)$. The expressions are identical, so the system is time invariant.

sections.section_title: Nonmatching Shift-Then-System and System-Then-Shift Expressions

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=x(t)+2t$, use the same shift test to classify whether the system is time invariant.
Let $y_1(t)=T\{x(t-T)\}$ and $y_2(t)=y(t-T)$, then choose the statement that matches this computation.

choice_blocks.text: The expressions do not match: $y_1(t)=x(t-T)+2t$ and $y_2(t)=x(t-T)+2(t-T)$. The system is time varying.
The expressions match exactly: $y_1(t)=x(t-T)+2t= y_2(t)=x(t-T)+2(t-T)$.
Only $y_1(t)$ is needed, so one-path agreement is enough to declare invariance.
They differ only by switching $T\to -T$ in the input argument, which does not affect invariance.
$y_1(t)=x(t+T)+2t$ and $y_2(t)=x(t-T)+2(t-T)$, so this is the time-invariant case.

questions.correct_answer: The system is time varying because $y_1(t)$ and $y_2(t)$ differ by an explicit-time term.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shift-first result is $y_1(t)=x(t-T)+2t$, while the shifted-output result is $y_2(t)=x(t-T)+2(t-T)$. The additive explicit-time term changes under system output shifting.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=x(t)+t^2$, compute both paths for arbitrary shift $T$ and classify the system.
Which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Not time invariant: $t^2$ does not shift the same way as $(t-T)^2$ in the two paths.
Time invariant because both expressions become $x(t-T)+t^2$.
Only non-matching when $T\neq0$, so the system is mostly time invariant.
Time invariant because the input and output both include shifted terms with $T$.
No classification is possible without substituting a numeric value of $T$.

questions.correct_answer: The system is time varying because explicit-time terms change under output shifting.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shift-first path keeps the explicit term as $t^2$, while the shifted output path uses $(t-T)^2$, so the expressions are unequal for arbitrary $T$.

sections.section_title: Testing Equality for an Arbitrary Input Shift

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=t x(t-3)$ and an input shift $x(t-T)$, which comparison is correct after computing the two paths for the time-invariance test?

choice_blocks.text: $y_1(t)=t x(t-T-3)$ and $y_2(t)=(t-T) x(t-T-3)$, so the paths are different and the system is time varying.
$y_1(t)=t x(t-T-3)$ and $y_2(t)=t x(t-T-3)$, so the system is time invariant.
Only the arguments are compared, so the two paths match when the argument becomes $x(t-T-3)$; therefore this is time invariant.
$y_1(t)=t x(t-T+3)$ and $y_2(t)=(t-T) x(t-T-3)$, which is a false match caused by using $T$ in the wrong sign position.
The two expressions are equal only for $T=0$, so the system is time invariant for that case.

questions.correct_answer: $y_1(t)=t x(t-T-3)$ and $y_2(t)=(t-T) x(t-T-3)$, so the system is time varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $x(t-T)$ into the system to get $y_1(t)=t x((t-T)-3)$. Then shift the original output, $y(t)=t x(t-3)$, by $T$ to get $y_2(t)=(t-T) x((t-T)-3)$. The factor changes from $t$ to $t-T$, so the expressions are not equal for arbitrary $T$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=(t+1)x(t+2)$ under input shift $x(t-T)$, which statement correctly compares the two time-invariance paths?

choice_blocks.text: $y_1(t)=(t+1)x(t-T+2)$ and $y_2(t)=(t-T+1)x(t-T+2)$, so the prefactor mismatch shows the system is time varying.
$y_1(t)=(t+1)x(t-T+2)$ and $y_2(t)=(t+1)x(t-T+2)$, so the two paths are equal.
The paths differ only by one argument sign, but this is the same as comparing $y(t)=y(t-T)$, so the system is not time varying.
$y_1(t)=t+1$ and $y_2(t)=(t+1)-T$, so the rule itself matches and the system is time invariant.
$y_1(t)=(t+1)x(t+2-T)$ and $y_2(t)=(t-T+1)x(t+2-T)$, so only the internal shift changes and the system is time invariant.

questions.correct_answer: $y_1(t)=(t+1)x(t-T+2)$ and $y_2(t)=(t-T+1)x(t-T+2)$; the mismatch in the prefactor means the system is time varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For the shift-then-system path, replace $x(t)$ by $x(t-T)$ to get $y_1(t)=(t+1)x((t-T)+2)=(t+1)x(t-T+2)$. For system-then-shift, write $y(t)=(t+1)x(t+2)$ and then evaluate $y(t-T)=(t-T+1)x((t-T)+2)$. The prefactor is not identical, so the paths do not match for arbitrary $T$.

sections.section_title: Classifying Time Invariance from Simplified Path Expressions

prompt_blocks.text: For $y_1(t)=x(t-T+2)$ and $y_2(t)=x(t-T+2)$, which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Time invariant, because the two path expressions are identical for all $T$.
Time varying, because a nonzero shift is present.
Time varying, because only the coefficient-free argument must be compared numerically.
Inconclusive, because the test is correct only for $T=1$.
Time invariant only if $y_1$ and $y_2$ are plotted and checked.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The two simplified paths are exactly the same, so they match term by term for every shift parameter. That is the direct condition for time invariance in this lesson format.

prompt_blocks.text: A test output gives $y_1(t)=2x(t+T-4)$ and $y_2(t)=2x((t-4)+T)$. Which is the best classification?

choice_blocks.text: Time invariant, since the two expressions are algebraically the same after simplifying $y_2(t)=2x(t+T-4)$.
Time varying, because the two paths look different before simplification.
Time varying, because matching requires checking only one signal value, such as at $T=0$.
Time invariant only if the output has no multiplicative factor, so this factor of 2 makes it noninvariant.
Cannot classify from simplified expressions; a direct time-domain derivation of $y(t)$ is required first.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both paths simplify to the same form, $2x(t+T-4)$, so no mismatch appears in argument, multiplier, or structure. That equality across all $T$ is the required condition.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the time-invariance shift test to memoryless continuous-time system rules by verifying that the fixed pointwise mapping from x(t) to y(t) commutes with input shifts and contains no explicit dependence on t.

sections.section_title: Testing a Constant-Gain Memoryless Rule

prompt_blocks.text: Test $y(t)=4x(t)$ with $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$. Which comparison is correct for the time-invariance test?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{tts}(t)=4x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=4x(t-T)$, so the two paths match and the rule is time invariant.
$y_{tts}(t)=4x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=4x(t-T)$; the sign change in one side means the rule is time varying.
$y_{tts}(t)=x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=4x(t-T)$; the missing gain on the shifted input side makes the system time varying.
$y_{tts}(t)=4x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=4x(t+T)$, so the shift direction changed between paths.
$y_{tts}(t)=4x(t)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=4x(t-T)$, so the gain changes only after shifting the output.

questions.correct_answer: $y_{tts}(t)=4x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=4x(t-T)$, so the system is time invariant.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: First, use the shifted input $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$. The shift-then-system path is $y_{tts}(t)=4x_T(t)=4x(t-T)$. From the original $y(t)=4x(t)$, shifting the output gives $y_{sts}(t)=4x(t-T)$. The two paths are identical, so this constant-gain memoryless rule is time invariant.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t)$, which statement is the correct result of the shift test using $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$?

choice_blocks.text: $y_{tts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$, so the system is time invariant.
$y_{tts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t+T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$, so the sign in the shift is reversed.
$y_{tts}(t)= -\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$, so the gain changed sign between paths.
$y_{tts}(t)=x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$, so the shifted-input path skipped the gain.
$y_{tts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t+T)$, so the output is shifted in opposite directions.

questions.correct_answer: $y_{tts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$ and $y_{sts}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$, so the system is time invariant.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shifted input is $x_T(t)=x(t-T)$, so $y_{tts}(t)=T\{x_T(t)\}=-\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$. The original output is $y(t)=-\frac{3}{2}x(t)$, and shifting it by $T$ gives $y_{sts}(t)= -\frac{3}{2}x(t-T)$. The expressions match exactly, so this rule remains time invariant.

sections.section_title: Testing a Squaring Memoryless Rule
